name: Papal political authority under Gregory the Great
plain_explanation: Before Gregory, the Bishop of Rome had prestige but no real authority outside his own diocese; Gregory, through skillful use of letters and diplomacy amid the political chaos of his time, made the papacy a genuine governing power across the Western Church and beyond.
precise_definition: The expansion, under Gregory the Great (590-604), of papal jurisdiction from a merely honorific primacy to an authority actively exercised, chiefly by extensive correspondence, over bishops and secular rulers across the former Western Empire, and acknowledged to a lesser degree even in the East.
why_it_mattered: It established the practical machinery -- correspondence, doctrinal instruction (the Book of Pastoral Rule), diplomatic pressure on barbarian kings -- through which the medieval papacy would later assert and expand its authority over secular rulers.
historical_origin: Enabled partly by Gregory's own political skill and partly by the prevailing anarchy of the period: Lombard ravages in Italy, anarchy in Spain and Africa, wars in France, and pagan reversion in Britain after the Saxon invasion.
examples: Gregory's Book of Pastoral Rule, used to instruct bishops through Charlemagne's time and translated into Anglo-Saxon by Alfred the Great
His extensive correspondence reproving bishops (e.g., the aged bishop of Cagliari) and advising barbarian sovereigns (Brunichild, Agilulph, Theodelinda)
competing_positions: Saint Ambrose's earlier position, in which even a Pope's friend never regarded himself as subject to papal authority outside his own see
influence_on_later_thinkers: Set the pattern the medieval Western Church would follow in asserting authority over secular princes.
